article.headline: The Hidden Tax Trap Lurking Inside a Cheap SK Hynix Trade
article.lede: SK Square looks like a backdoor into SK Hynix at a steep discount — but for U.S. investors, the wrapper may come with a punishing tax classification that erases the apparent arbitrage before a single share is sold.
article.body:
There is a version of the SK Square trade that sounds almost too elegant. SK Square (KRX: 402340), the Seoul-based holding company spun out of SK Telecom in 2021, derives more than 96% of its net asset value from a 20.1% equity stake in SK Hynix — currently one of the most consequential semiconductor companies on the planet — yet trades at a discount to that underlying stake of anywhere from 25% to 47%, depending on the period. Buying SK Square, in this framing, is tantamount to purchasing SK Hynix shares at a substantial markdown. NH Investment & Securities found the logic compelling enough to raise its target price for SK Square to 1.1 million won in April 2026, a 49% upward revision from its prior estimate, as the NAV discount narrowed and Hynix's earnings reached historic highs. But the discount exists for reasons, and for American investors one of the most consequential is tax law.

The IRS classifies certain foreign corporations as Passive Foreign Investment Companies, or PFICs — a designation invented in 1986 to prevent U.S. taxpayers from sheltering income inside low-tax offshore vehicles. The rules apply a two-part test annually. A foreign company is a PFIC if 75% or more of its gross income is *passive* — dividends, interest, rents, royalties, or capital gains — or if at least 50% of its average assets are passive-income-producing. A pure holding company, whose primary "income" consists of dividends received from subsidiaries and whose assets consist almost entirely of publicly traded equity stakes, sits squarely in the crosshairs. SK Square's portfolio, for all its strategic branding, is economically closer to a closed-end fund than an operating business; whether its income formally clears the 75% passive-income threshold is a question for a qualified tax attorney, but the structural risk is high enough that the poster treats it as effectively certain.

The tax consequences of PFIC status are deliberately punitive. The default regime — the *excess distribution method* — taxes any distribution exceeding 125% of the three-year average at the highest ordinary income rate applicable in each year of the holding period, rather than the 15–20% long-term capital gains rate that applies to most equity investments. The mechanism is worse on disposition: gains from selling PFIC stock are allocated ratably across the entire holding period, taxed at the top marginal rate for each historical year, and then subjected to an additional interest charge that approximates what the IRS calculates it would have earned had the tax been paid as it accrued. The longer the position is held, the more compounding interest accumulates on top of already-elevated ordinary income tax rates. The result is an effective rate that can substantially exceed 37% once the interest surcharge is layered in — a remarkable outcome on what is nominally a capital gain.

Alternative elections exist but impose their own frictions. The *QEF election* — short for Qualified Electing Fund — requires the PFIC to provide annual ordinary earnings and net capital gain statements in a specific IRS-prescribed format; most Korean issuers do not supply this documentation, and investors cannot make the election unilaterally without it. The *mark-to-market election*, available for PFICs listed on a qualified exchange, taxes annual appreciation as ordinary income rather than deferring it, which at least avoids the interest-charge problem but forfeits capital gains treatment entirely. Neither route restores the economics of simply owning SK Hynix directly through its listed shares (KRX: 000660 or 000660.KS on global platforms). And then there is the compliance drag: IRS Form 8621, the annual information return required from every U.S. PFIC shareholder, must be filed for each PFIC position, and the professional cost typically runs $200 to $500 per form per year — a recurring friction that compounds alongside the investment itself.

The underlying asset that makes SK Square interesting is unambiguously exceptional. SK Hynix reported record Q1 2026 revenue of 52.6 trillion won, up 198% year-over-year, with an operating margin of 72% and net income that exceeded revenue from a year prior. The company commands roughly 57% of the global HBM — *high-bandwidth memory*, the stacked DRAM architecture that feeds the insatiable data appetite of AI accelerators — market, a position it has defended through manufacturing leadership in 4-nanometer packaging processes. Its cash position reached 54.3 trillion won against debt of 19.3 trillion won, a net cash posture that is itself extraordinary for a cyclical memory maker. The AI memory supercycle that analysts have long anticipated is, in SK Hynix's financial statements, now empirically present rather than merely projected.

The practical upshot for U.S. investors is straightforward, if slightly counterintuitive: the more compelling the underlying thesis, the more important it becomes to own the asset in the most tax-efficient wrapper. SK Hynix's own shares are listed on the KRX and accessible through most brokerages that offer international trading; they do not carry the PFIC risk that haunts the SK Square holding structure, because SK Hynix is an operating semiconductor manufacturer rather than a passive investment vehicle. The apparent NAV discount at SK Square is real, but for an American taxpayer paying ordinary income rates on gains plus an IRS interest surcharge, a discount that looks like 35–47% on a pre-tax basis may look far thinner — or negative — on an after-tax one. The lesson is an old one in international investing: the price you pay for an asset and the price the government takes when you sell it are two entirely separate negotiations, and conflating them is the kind of mistake that holds up well in a bull market and badly in everything else.

concepts.definition: An IRS designation for a foreign corporation that earns 75% or more of its gross income from passive sources (dividends, interest, rents, royalties, capital gains) or holds 50% or more of its assets in passive-income-producing investments. PFIC status triggers punitive tax treatment on gains and distributions for U.S. shareholders.

The annual information return U.S. persons must file for each PFIC they hold. Required when receiving distributions from a PFIC, recognizing gain on a disposition, or making various PFIC elections. Professional preparation typically costs $200–$500 per form per year.

The IRS default tax regime for PFICs. Distributions exceeding 125% of the three-year average, and all gains on disposition, are allocated across the holding period and taxed at the highest ordinary income rate for each year, plus a compounding interest charge on deferred taxes.

The gap between a holding company's market price and its net asset value — the sum of its underlying stakes. SK Square has historically traded at a 25–47% discount to the value of its SK Hynix stake and other assets.

A stacked DRAM architecture that vertically layers memory chips and connects them with microscopic through-silicon vias, dramatically increasing the speed and bandwidth available to AI accelerators. SK Hynix holds approximately 57% global HBM market share.

An IRS opt-in that avoids the PFIC excess distribution penalty by taxing the investor's pro-rata share of a PFIC's ordinary earnings and net capital gains each year. Requires the foreign company to provide specific IRS-format earnings statements — documentation most Korean issuers do not supply.
